segments.t: Why did you do it?
Well, I felt it was an opportunity to buy a business that is going to be around for
a hundred or two hundred years, that's interwoven with the American economy in a way that if
the American economy prospers, the business will prosper.
It is the most efficient way of moving goods in the country.
It's the most environmentally friendly way of moving goods, and both those things are
going to be very important.
But the biggest thing is, the United States is going to do well.
We can't move the railroad to China or India, at least I've figured out.
So it's a little like the river for that song about New York.
We have to make it here or we can't make it anywhere.
But it does move a ton of goods, 470 miles on one gallon of diesel.
A train replaces 280 trucks on the road, and it emits far less into the atmosphere that's
damaging than truckings, and when I'm talking about the whole rail industry, it moves 40%
of the goods plus.
And you have new port of entries like Houston that will bring in a lot of goods through
the Panama Canal.
And we're going to have more people in this country, and they're going to be using more
goods over time.
And sure, there's a bad year from time to time, and in the next hundred years, there'll
probably be 15 bad years, and I don't know what order they'll appear, but I also know
the railroads will be essential to the country.
Now, when you called Charlie Munger and said, I'm thinking about this, did he say right
on Warren, or did he say, how about this?
Well, if Charlie said right on Warren, I figured I had the wrong number, no, I mean, that would
be the wrong number.
It's not likely.
That might be my wife or my, you know, but Charlie gave it kind of a low-level grumble,
and that is a real endorsement from Charlie.
But I mean, he also pointed out, it is said that, you know, this was a regulated industry,
this was an industry that was capital intensive, this was an industry that was unionized.
